4. Stochastic and Stochastic 2: netSD, time, energy and algorithmic complexity

4.0. Which model and which computation?

This section describes both published models: Stochastic and Stochastic 2. The charts in 4.2–4.7 benchmark the shared netSD scoring kernel with 4,096 candidates. They report neither model’s full optimisation time or energy, nor newly optimised portfolios. Model results and separately measured saved-policy evaluation appear in 4.8; the complexity study is in 4.9.

Stochastic 2 uses a conditional 20-state price-template model with smoothed rare transitions. More scenarios do not by themselves guarantee a better forecast or policy. No-sale: 9 root-stage candidates scored; Main: 61 root-stage candidates scored; Sale: 200 root-stage candidates scored. Matching initial allocations do not prove that the optimal solutions are identical.

Actual optimisation time versus a scoring benchmark

The seconds in the scoring and saved-policy tables are not the time needed to find a portfolio. Full optimisation repeatedly generates, repairs and scores candidates across decision nodes and policy variants. A saved-policy evaluation only scores an already chosen strategy, after shared preparation and warmup.

A GPU process is not a CUDA core. The experiment holds GPU ownership at one process and changes batch size to measure useful device parallelism. Multiple competing CUDA processes were not benchmarked; no GPU process-count sensitivity is claimed. Launching many GPU contexts would duplicate memory and add contention. CPU workers can perform other supported work alongside the GPU owner.

4.4. Measurement method, correctness and memory

Measured points and fitted scalability curves

CPU and GPU share 8 numeric settings: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48, 60. CPU stops at the requested maximum of 60 processes. Additional GPU-only batch sizes: 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. Every point evaluates the same 4096 candidates, with the same prices, histories, references, precision and six outputs. The GPU-only extension does not invent CPU measurements or extrapolate the CPU curve beyond 60.

64 to 60 fallback: Windows/Python rejected 64 workers: max_workers must be <= 61. The authorised alternative of 60 actual CPU processes was measured; GPU includes the same 60-candidate batch setting. No 64-process CPU result is invented.

Axis meanings differ: n CPU processes versus B candidate portfolios per call to one GPU owner. Matching \(n=B\) provides matched numeric sampling points, not equivalent hardware resources or numbers of GPU cores/processes. GPU acceleration in the comparison column is \(\frac{T_{\mathrm{CPU}}(n)}{T_{\mathrm{GPU}}(B=n)}\); ratios below 1 favour CPU. CPU processes are not left computing during timed GPU runs. Startup and warmup remain outside the timed work; GPU calls include transfers and are synchronised.

BackendCurveFitted time equationParametersR² (time)R² (log time)Held-out RMS log errorHeld-out MAPE
CPUAmdahl\(T_{\mathrm A}(n)\)\(s=0.00795043\)0.999790.996400.105318.89%
CPUUSL (CV selected)\(T_{\mathrm{USL}}(n)\)\(\alpha=1.99611\times10^{-18}\)
\(\beta=0.000170542\)		0.999980.999070.051513.58%
GPULaunch amortisation (CV selected)\(T_{\mathrm L}(B)\)a_seconds=0.312145; b_seconds_per_call=0.01023290.991420.994370.1298511.68%
GPUSaturating power\(T_{\mathrm P}(B)\)a_seconds=0.346584; b_seconds=47.4272; k=1.06530.967650.996020.1362511.47%

CPU models. Amdahl: \(S_{\mathrm A}(n)=\frac{1}{s+(1-s)/n}\), with effective serial fraction s. Universal Scalability Law (USL): \(S_{\mathrm{USL}}(n)=\frac{n}{1+\alpha(n-1)+\beta n(n-1)}\), allowing contention and a coordination penalty. T1 is the measured one-process CPU median, held fixed. Nonnegative parameters are constrained to their stated model domains; an effective fitted parameter is not a direct hardware profiling measurement.

GPU models. Launch amortisation: \(T_{\mathrm L}(B)=a+b\left\lceil\frac{W}{B}\right\rceil\), where \(W=4096\) and \(\lceil W/B\rceil\) counts calls. The empirical saturating generalisation \(T_{\mathrm P}(B)=a+\frac{b}{B^k}\) allows a different decay rate; it is a descriptive alternative, not a physical scalability law. These batch models are motivated by per-call/transfer overhead and do not treat batch size as a processor count. Gustafson’s law concerns growing problem size per processor, so it is described as a common weak-scaling model rather than fitted to this fixed-workload experiment.

Fit and validation. Nonlinear least squares minimises log-time residuals. Models are selected by the lowest leave-one-setting-out RMS log-time error; the entire setting is held out, not an individual repeated timing. For CPU, n=1 remains a fixed anchor and is excluded from held-out scoring. MAPE is the mean absolute held-out percentage time error; R² is shown for raw and log times. Min–max bars describe repeat variation, not confidence intervals. No high-order polynomial or extrapolated optimal processor count is asserted. Three repeats and one machine do not capture all thermal, clock or background-load variation.

Primary sources: NVIDIA: strong/weak scaling, Amdahl and Gustafson; Neil J. Gunther: Universal Scalability Law; NVIDIA: batching transfer overhead. Amortisation equations above are the explicitly stated modelling choices for these measurements.

Times are medians of three measurement-window averages per completed 4096-candidate invocation; each window lasts at least 3 seconds and may contain different numbers of identical invocations, reported in the energy table; min–max shows repeat variation. CPU measurements use actual Windows spawned processes, with their initial loading/JIT shown separately; timed work includes task scheduling and result collection. GPU measurements include host/device transfers, sorting, matrix multiplication and counts, after CUDA warmup. CPU and GPU measurements are sequential, not simultaneous. Machine load and workload size affect results; startup-adjusted CPU totals are shown explicitly. Every measured CPU and GPU result matched the same baseline exactly for all six counts.

Additional validation: 256 real-history candidate portfolios, 66 synthetic dominance cases, price-path agreement within 1e-12 relative/absolute tolerance, Numba CUDA JIT and PyTorch GPU backpropagation. Software: PyTorch 2.12.0+cu126; CuPy 14.2.0. CUDA-dependent libraries are isolated from the original CPU environment.

System RAM is polled every second. At 88% observed usage, only the owned task tree is stopped and retried with half as many CPU workers. The 2% margin targets the 90% ceiling; polling cannot guarantee a hard ceiling against sudden allocations or unrelated programs. VRAM batches adapt to free memory, retaining 512 MiB and limiting the CuPy pool to at most 95% of device memory. Dominance batches shrink after allocation failure. These are memory budgets, not measured GPU utilisation percentages.

Current timing and energy tables use the same requested CPU/GPU sampling grid and the same completed workload; raw energy counter endpoints and repetition counts are preserved for audit.

CPU energy models use the engineering identity \(E=P\,T\) with an effective linear power model, and an empirical reciprocal-plus-overhead alternative. GPU models use per-call energy amortisation and a saturating power-law alternative. These are descriptive engineering fits, not Landauer-limit measurements. Both raw-unit and log-unit R² are shown; model selection uses leave-one-setting-out RMS log-energy error. For the \(E=P\,T\) model the time curve is held fixed from the timing experiment, so its energy CV is conditional on that fitted time curve, not a fully independent validation of the entire two-stage model. All curves stop within measured ranges.

Literature context: Gunther: USL and its Amdahl/Gustafson relationships; NVIDIA: strong scaling and batching overhead; Konopik et al., Nature Communications (2023): parallelism, overhead and energy. The final article provides theoretical context; its fundamental thermodynamic model is not asserted to fit this workstation.

4.8. Both models: netSD, time and energy side by side

New saved-policy evaluation measured at: 2026-11-13T07:27:44.815887+02:00 (Europe/Vilnius).

Three different netSD measures. The initial-allocation historical netSD in 1.1 does not evaluate later trades. Below, diagnostic E[netSD] is the published optimisation objective: the historical sample with final-decision weights and 20 future daily returns, scored per branch and probability-weighted. Terminal netSD is the newly calculated FSD/SSD/TSD score of the whole policy’s four-week cumulative-return distribution, including every intermediate trade and cash. This is a separate evaluation; portfolios were not reoptimised for it.

The terminal comparison uses scenario probabilities, 70 individual assets and Current including remaining cash; every row uses the same maximum denominator \(D=3\times71=213\), distinct from the historical diagnostic \(D=114\). The calculation uses the weighted empirical CDF and its integrals; average daily returns do not replace the horizon-return distribution.

Discrete dominance counts can change near equal CDF or integral differences. This measures numerical classification sensitivity, not a forecast confidence interval.

This compares each model on its own scenarios; it is not a financial ranking under a common scenario distribution. Stochastic uses 20 representative paths and full future revelation; Stochastic 2 uses 160,000 smoothed conditional outcomes and causal decisions. Differences in netSD therefore reflect forecasting, information and search differences. A policy-performance test would require a common external scenario set and predefined rules for applying each policy outside its own tree. A higher diagnostic score or lower resource cost alone does not establish a better investment policy.

Scope of the time and energy table: saved-policy re-evaluation, including terminal netSD, after input loading, shared reference preparation and JIT/CUDA warmup. Original Stochastic: three windows of at least 3 seconds, each repeating the complete 20-outcome workload; Stochastic 2: one full 160,000-outcome evaluation per distinct policy. These are not search-energy measurements or equal-workload speed-up comparisons. Identical policies share the same measurement; these are not independent repeats. Up to 48 CPU threads; Stochastic ran on CPU, Stochastic 2 on CPU and one CUDA process. Energy is the total increase in CPU-package and GPU-board hardware counters, including background activity and idle GPU energy during CPU work. It is not an isolated-process or whole-system wall measurement. The wall model adds 80 W and assumes 90% PSU efficiency and 200 g CO₂e/kWh; these are illustrative assumptions, not Lithuanian grid measurements.

4.9. Algorithmic complexity

Notation: \(A=70\) assets, \(H=1129\) historical observations, \(T=20\) days, \(M=H+T=1149\), \(R=71\) references, S is the terminal scenario count, N the decision-node count, d the number of decision stages, P the candidate limit per node, and I the sweep count.

ComponentTime complexity / growthMeaning in this implementation
One daily-return netSD evaluation\(C_{\mathrm{SD}}\)Candidate sorting and R linear CDF/integral merges. Third-order SD is not \(\mathcal O(M^3)\).
One policy evaluation\(C_{\mathrm{eval}}\)Historical/future portfolio returns and all comparisons. Stochastic 2 shares the historical component across 20 terminal siblings.
Terminal netSD\(C_{\mathrm{terminal}}\)Weighted terminal-return distributions; historical daily observations are not appended here.
Bounded node search\(C_{\mathrm{search}}\)\(C_{\mathrm{leaf}}\) is one outcome evaluation; \(C_{\mathrm{repair}}\) is integer-feasibility repair. An earlier change can affect an entire subtree.
Full uniformly branching tree\(S,\ N\)\(b=20,\ d=4\): 160,000 outcomes and 8,421 decision nodes. With fixed b, growth is exponential in the number of stages.
Enumeration of all quantity combinations\(K_{\max}\)An enumeration upper bound, not this heuristic’s runtime formula.
Dense references for all outcomes\(B_{\mathrm{ref}}\)Stochastic 2 does not keep this as one GPU array: references are streamed and prices are memory-mapped.
Price matrix / policy quantities\(B_{\mathrm{prices}},\ B_q\)About 1.75 GiB for prices and 4.50 MiB for quantities; this is not total process RAM.

Sources of complexity: general integer budget selection is related to combinatorial problems such as knapsack; netSD has discrete dominance thresholds and an irregular integer feasible region. No formal NP-hardness proof for this exact netSD formulation is claimed here. The heuristic guarantees neither an exact optimiser’s polynomial runtime nor an optimal solution. Unit-by-unit budget repair can also depend on numerical quantity bounds. The fixed shortlist of 8 assets and 2 sweeps limits work but can leave better root decisions unexplored.

CPU and GPU change constants and the parallelisable fraction, not \(b^d\) scenario growth or the combinatorial selection problem. The Amdahl bound \(\frac{1}{f+(1-f)/p}\) applies only to fixed work and a specified serial fraction f; GPU transfers, data preparation and Python repair reduce practical speed-up. These measurements do not identify f or the full-search speed-up.

Theoretical background: Karp: Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems; Shapiro: Stochastic Programming Approach to Optimization under Uncertainty; Amdahl (1967). The cost expressions above analyse this implementation; they are not claims by these sources about this portfolio.

Controlled empirical scoring-kernel scaling study

One of M, R or S varies while the others remain fixed; one CPU thread, synthetic return samples and the same six dominance counts. This is not model optimisation or a process-count experiment. Three short repetition windows of at least 0.15 s per point; error bars show min–max, not confidence intervals. Short-window energy measurements are more sensitive to counter resolution and background activity. Theoretical forms with nonnegative coefficients and a power curve are fitted; R² is descriptive, without a held-out sample, and does not prove asymptotic complexity.

4.10. Equations in LaTeX

Tables use short function symbols; the full expressions are shown here. The mathematical model and numerical results are unchanged.

Time and energy curves

\[T_{\mathrm A}(n)=T_1\!\left(s+\frac{1-s}{n}\right)\]
\[T_{\mathrm{USL}}(n)=\frac{T_1}{n}\left[1+\alpha(n-1)+\beta n(n-1)\right]\]
\[T_{\mathrm L}(B)=a+b\left\lceil\frac{W}{B}\right\rceil\]
\[T_{\mathrm P}(B)=a+\frac{b}{B^k}\]
\[E_{\mathrm{PT}}(n)=(P_0+P_1n)T(n)\]
\[E_{\mathrm R}(n)=a+\frac{b}{n}+cn\]
\[E_{\mathrm L}(B)=a+b\left\lceil\frac{W}{B}\right\rceil\]
\[E_{\mathrm P}(B)=a+\frac{b}{B^k}\]
\[\begin{aligned}S_{\mathrm A}(n)&=\frac{1}{s+(1-s)/n},\\S_{\mathrm{USL}}(n)&=\frac{n}{1+\alpha(n-1)+\beta n(n-1)}\end{aligned}\]

Energy, cost and environmental-impact assumptions

\[E_{\mathrm{socket},J}=\frac{E_{\mathrm{CPU},J}+E_{\mathrm{GPU},J}+P_{\mathrm{other}}t}{\eta}\]
\[E_{\mathrm{socket},\mathrm{kWh}}=\frac{E_{\mathrm{socket},J}}{3.6\times10^6}\]
\[\mathrm{Cost}_{\mathrm{EUR}}=E_{\mathrm{socket},\mathrm{kWh}}\,c_{\mathrm{EUR/kWh}}\]
\[G_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}=E_{\mathrm{socket},\mathrm{kWh}}\,g_{\mathrm{CO_2e/kWh}}\]

netSD and terminal valuation

\[\begin{aligned}V_T^{(s)}&=(p_T^{(s)})^{\!\top}q_{\mathrm{last}}^{(s)}+c_{\mathrm{last}}^{(s)},\\R_T^{(s)}&=\frac{V_T^{(s)}}{V_0}-1\end{aligned}\]
\[\widehat F_\pi(x)=\sum_{s=1}^{S}p_s\,\mathbf1\{R_{T,\pi}^{(s)}\le x\}\]
\[\mathrm{netSD}_{T,\pi}=\frac{\mathrm{OUT}_{T,\pi}-\mathrm{IN}_{T,\pi}}{D},\qquad D=3\cdot71=213\]
\[\mathbb E[\mathrm{netSD}_{\mathrm{diag}}]=\sum_{s=1}^{S}p_s\,\mathrm{netSD}_{\mathrm{diag}}^{(s)}\]

Complexity and curve fitting

\[C_{\mathrm{SD}}\in\mathcal O(M\log M+RM)\]
\[\begin{aligned}C_{\mathrm{eval}}\in\mathcal O\bigl(&S[(H+T)A\\&+M\log M+RM]\bigr)\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}C_{\mathrm{ref}}&\in\mathcal O(RS\log S),\\C_{\mathrm{terminal}}&\in\mathcal O(S\log S+RS)\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}C_{\mathrm{search}}\in\mathcal O\bigl(&Id(P+1)S C_{\mathrm{leaf}}\\&+IPdN C_{\mathrm{repair}}\bigr)\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}S&=b^d,\\N&=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}b^j=\frac{b^d-1}{b-1}\quad(b>1)\end{aligned}\]
\[K_{\max}=(U+1)^{AN},\qquad q_{n,i}\in\{0,\ldots,U\}\]
\[B_{\mathrm{ref}}=8SRM\;\mathrm{bytes}\approx97.2\;\mathrm{GiB}\]
\[\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{prices}}&=8S(T+1)A\;\mathrm{bytes},\\B_q&=8AN\;\mathrm{bytes}\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}\widehat y_M&=c_0+c_1(M\log_2M+71M),\\\widehat y_x&=c_0+c_1x,\\\widehat y_{\mathrm{power}}&=a\,x^k\end{aligned}\]
\[R^2=1-\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2}{\sum_i(y_i-\overline y)^2}\]

Isolated calibration pause: run 20261112_stage1000_technology7108_cpu48 was paused for 338.67 seconds during the controlled CPU48/CUDA experiments in 4.12, then resumed. Its invocation elapsed time retains that pause, and its gross hardware energy includes the calibration. This invocation is not an uninterrupted solver-speed benchmark; calibration windows must not be added again to its energy.

Scenario-layout validation pause: run 20261112_stage1000_technology7108_cpu48 retained 506.39 seconds of controlled local/live browser checks while its numerical writer was suspended and later resumed. Invocation wall time and gross hardware counters include this maintenance interval; it is not numerical search throughput.

Attractiveness validation pause: run 20261112_stage1000_technology7108_cpu48 retained 552.75 seconds of local/live research browser checks while its numerical writer was suspended and later resumed. Invocation wall time and gross hardware counters include this maintenance interval; it is not numerical search throughput.

CPU batch trial pause: run 20261112_vlp87_cpu48 retained 18.11 seconds while its numerical writer was suspended for the isolated packet-scheduling trial in 4.12 and then resumed. Invocation wall time and gross hardware counters include this interval; its trial energy must not be added again.

Progressive-publication pauses: run 20261112_vlp87_cpu48 retained 2612.38 seconds in 4 controlled pipeline pauses for publishing and checking completed parts. Its continuous wall time and the affected invocation hardware counters include these intervals. They are maintenance time, not isolated numerical throughput; overlapping publication energy must not be added again.

Interrupted run and reduced CPU limit: Windows recorded MEMORY_MANAGEMENT 0x1A / 0x41792 (a corrupted page-table entry) on 12 November 2026. Production now uses 48 CPU workers; earlier 60-worker observations retain their original counts. The last valid RAM-monitor reading was about 13%; the final audit did not survive the reboot, so the crash-time maximum is unknown. The exact hardware or driver cause is unconfirmed. Reducing worker count reduces load and does not establish that the fault is repaired. Recovered policies are independently rescored before use; interrupted energy without final counters remains unmeasured.

Archived counterfactual: the following SAF test predates the latest confirmed holding changes. Its snapshot has VLP1L 42 rather than the current 87; these scores do not describe the latest portfolio.

Sale-permission counterfactual: SAF1R

The former Sale variant required technical SELL votes and a negative forecast. The user removed those requirements at every decision on 11 November 2026. No-sale still prohibits all sales. The following is a controlled counterfactual under the original Stochastic scenario law, before reoptimising the broader Sale model. Initial SAF proceeds stay as cash. The repaired case makes the additional small holding changes needed to retain the 30% sector cap; the unrepaired case violates that cap in two nodes and is not a feasible candidate. These three netSD definitions are distinct.

4.12. CPU48 and CUDA: measured workload balance

Measured 2026-11-12T13:09:11.342852+02:00 on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti. CPU parallelism is 48 Numba worker threads with the GIL released; CUDA uses one active owner process per workload. The paused previous model remains resident during calibration. GPU share means the fraction of independent scoring jobs assigned to CUDA, not a number of GPU processes. CPU work and CUDA work overlap. The previous implementation assigned 35% to CUDA without calibration.

Each setting uses identical candidate arrays, reference distributions, return lengths and output counts. Shared, scenario and unique patterns use batches of 64, 256, 640 and 1024 jobs. The additional node pattern uses 1024, 4096, 8192 and 16384 jobs with 320 reference IDs (640 for the largest batch), reproducing the large reused-reference batches in the actual solver. Nine GPU shares (0, 10, 20, 35, 50, 65, 80, 90 and 100%) were measured in three randomly interleaved repeats after warmup. Every setting matched the CPU-only six directional FSD/SSD/TSD counts exactly. Shared means one reused reference set; scenario means twenty reused reference sets; unique means one distinct reference ID per job. Node and unique patterns use repeated frozen scenario templates to reproduce transfer volume and reuse rather than independent financial scenarios. Time includes host submission, CPU work, IPC, transfers, GPU sorting/scoring and collection. Feasibility repairs, model loading, optimisation search and report publication are outside these windows.

The selected share minimises the observed median time for each tested batch size and reference pattern. Other batch sizes use the nearest measured size on a logarithmic scale. This is a measured kernel scheduling choice, not proof of a global optimum or a whole-refresh speed-up. Deterministic tie-breaking and CPU winner verification remain unchanged. Full-run wall time and financial netSD are recorded separately in 4.8 and 4.11.

The calibrated scheduler is enabled for subsequent Stochastic 2 optimisation and its frozen-policy replay. The original two-stage Stochastic optimiser retains its CPU implementation; no GPU speed-up is claimed for that full optimiser. Only hardware scheduling changes: identical directional counts preserve the financial objective, penalties and netSD.

Each candidate has 1147 return observations and 71 reference distributions. Peak sampled system RAM during calibration: 13.20%; peak CUDA allocator pool across the calibration segments: 4.404 GiB. The previous writer was paused for isolation and resumed in a finally block, with an independent recovery watchdog. Its elapsed clock includes this pause; overlapping hardware energy windows must not be added together.

The descriptive time fit uses \(t(f)=a+\max\{b(1-f),cf\}\) with nonnegative coefficients; selection uses measured points, not the fitted minimum. Energy curves join measured points without claiming an energy model.
